title: Sort Colors (Dutch National Flag) — three pointers for 0s, 1s, 2s.
shortTitle: Sort Colors (Dutch National Flag) — Three Pointers for 0s, 1s, 2s

s1_definition.profdef: The Dutch National Flag algorithm sorts an array containing only three distinct values (0, 1, 2) in a single pass using three pointers: `low` marks the boundary of the 0 region, `high` marks the boundary of the 2 region, and `mid` scans the array. It partitions the array into zeros, ones, and twos in O(n) time and O(1) extra space without a general sort.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India classifies each pending request as low, medium, or high risk, coded 0, 1, 2. Instead of running a full sort, Rajesh sweeps once: anything low he swaps to the front, anything high he swaps to the back, and medium stays where it is, so the pile ends up grouped low then medium then high in one pass.
s1_definition.oneliner: Three pointers partition a 0/1/2 array in one pass — swap 0s to the front, 2s to the back, leave 1s in the middle.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Dutch National Flag algorithm sorts an array containing only three distinct values (0, 1, 2) in a single pass using three pointers: `low` marks the boundary of the 0 region, `high` marks the boundary of the 2 region, and `mid` scans the array. It partitions the array into zeros, ones, and twos in O(n) time and O(1) extra space without a general sort.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India classifies each pending request as low, medium, or high risk, coded 0, 1, 2. Instead of running a full sort, Rajesh sweeps once: anything low he swaps to the front, anything high he swaps to the back, and medium stays where it is, so the pile ends up grouped low then medium then high in one pass.

**One line to remember:** Three pointers partition a 0/1/2 array in one pass — swap 0s to the front, 2s to the back, leave 1s in the middle.

sections.s2_technical:
Initialize `low = 0`, `mid = 0`, `high = n - 1`. The loop runs while `mid <= high`. There are three cases based on `a[mid]`.

If `a[mid] == 0`, swap `a[low]` and `a[mid]`, then increment both `low` and `mid`, because the value coming from `low` is already processed (it can only be a 1 that we have seen). If `a[mid] == 1`, it is in its correct middle region, so just increment `mid`. If `a[mid] == 2`, swap `a[mid]` and `a[high]`, then decrement `high` only, and crucially do not increment `mid`, because the value swapped in from `high` is unexamined and must be checked next.

A code snippet classifying risk codes: `void sort012(int[] a) { int low=0, mid=0, high=a.length-1; while (mid<=high) { if (a[mid]==0) { swap(a,low++,mid++); } else if (a[mid]==1) { mid++; } else { swap(a,mid,high--); } } }`. The invariant is that everything before `low` is 0, everything between `low` and `mid` is 1, and everything after `high` is 2; the unknown region is between `mid` and `high`.

The nuance interviewers test is why `mid` does not advance after a 2-swap: the element brought from the high end has not been classified yet, so advancing `mid` would skip examining it and could leave a 0 stranded in the middle. The algorithm is a single linear pass, unlike counting sort which is also O(n) but needs two passes or extra counts; the Dutch flag is an elegant in-place one-pass partition and is the canonical answer when exactly three categories exist.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India fraud queue tags each pending transaction with a risk tier: 0 low, 1 medium, 2 high. The review tool must group them low-to-high so reviewers clear the safe ones quickly and escalate the risky ones, and it must do this in one pass on a large live queue. This is exactly how the Dutch National Flag algorithm works — three pointers partition the three tiers in a single sweep.

Problem 2 — The queue array is large and shared, so we sort in place without a second array or a general comparison sort.

The code shows a `RiskQueueSorter` with `sortByTier`, a demo on a mixed risk-tier array, and the grouped result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: risk tiers [2, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 2, 1].

Step 1: `low` 0, `mid` 0, `high` 8. `a[mid]` is 2, so swap `a[0]` and `a[8]` giving [1,0,1,2,1,0,0,2,2], decrement `high` to 7, `mid` stays 0 to re-examine the new value.

Step 2: `a[mid]` is now 1, so just advance `mid` to 1. `a[1]` is 0, so swap `a[low]` and `a[mid]` (both make 0 go front), increment `low` to 1 and `mid` to 2. The front now holds a 0.

Step 3: Scanning continues: 1s advance `mid`, 0s swap to the growing front region, and 2s swap to the shrinking back region without moving `mid`. Each 2-swap pulls an unexamined value into `mid` which is then classified on the next iteration.

Step 4: The unknown window between `mid` and `high` keeps shrinking. When `mid` passes `high`, every element has been placed in its correct region.

Step 5: The final array is grouped as all 0s, then all 1s, then all 2s: [0,0,0,1,1,1,2,2,2].

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Before: [2, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 2, 1]
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    After : [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [2,0,1,2,1,0,0,2,1]
    │
    ▼
  regions: [0s | 1s | unknown | 2s]
    │ a[mid]==0 → swap(low,mid), low++, mid++
    │ a[mid]==1 → mid++
    │ a[mid]==2 → swap(mid,high), high--  (mid stays)
    ▼
  Result: [0,0,0,1,1,1,2,2,2]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Dutch National Flag algorithm sorts an array that contains only three distinct values in a single linear pass using three pointers. A low pointer marks the end of the zero region, a high pointer marks the start of the two region, and a mid pointer scans the array. When the mid pointer sees a zero I swap it into the low region and advance both low and mid; when it sees a one I leave it and just advance mid; and when it sees a two I swap it into the high region and move the high pointer inward without advancing mid.

The detail that separates a correct implementation from a broken one is why mid does not move after swapping a two to the back. The value pulled in from the high end has not been classified yet, so if I advanced mid I could skip examining it and leave a zero stranded in the middle. Keeping mid in place forces that incoming value to be checked on the next iteration.

The reason I reach for this instead of a general sort is that it is a single in-place pass with constant extra space, whereas a comparison sort is order n log n and counting sort needs a second pass or extra counters. When there are exactly three categories, the Dutch flag is the canonical, optimal answer.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the fraud review tool. Each pending transaction carried a risk tier of low, medium, or high coded as zero, one, and two, and the tool needed to group a large live queue from low to high in one pass so reviewers could clear safe items fast and escalate risky ones. I sorted the shared queue array in place to avoid copying it. Explaining the three regions, the swap rules, and especially why mid stays put after a high swap shows the interviewer I understand the invariant that makes this one-pass partition correct.

---

keyPoints: Comparison sorts: merge sort O(n log n), quick sort O(n log n) average
Non-comparison: counting sort, radix sort — O(n) for limited range
Kth largest: quickselect O(n) average, heap O(n log k)
